title: Provoke AMLO
author: Alejandro Páez Varela
content:
_This article by[Alejandro Páez
Varela](https://www.sinembargo.mx/author/alejandro/) originally appeared in
the [October 5, 2026 edition of
SinEmbargo](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4881393/provoquen-a-amlo/), a Mexican
independent digital news outlet._

## 1\. The Worst Mistake of All

Andrés Manuel López Obrador often tells that after 2006, after the electoral
fraud and the end of the Reforma sit-in, the rain of mud against him had been
so thick that the right thought it had buried him in the mire. "They gave me
up for dead," he would say.

In his book _¡Gracias!_ (Planeta, 2024), AMLO recounts:

> "In the moments of greatest State violence in the country, without ceasing
> to denounce Calderón's mistaken and criminal strategy, I was able to come
> out unharmed from that authoritarian storm because, luckily, I decided to
> travel to every municipality in Mexico to raise awareness and organize the
> people from below; my tours at ground level saved me; since I met in the
> public plazas with few people, they believed I was finished and gave me up
> for dead, politically speaking. Calderón himself would say, when asked about
> me in interviews, that I was out there meeting with 10 or 20 people. In
> every sense, it was a miracle, because they did not bother with me, they let
> me work, and the visits to the towns and regions of Mexico were instructive
> and fundamental for the future of our movement."

I will never forget an interview with Claudio X. González senior looking at
the camera, his jaw trembling with hatred and making the "small" gesture with
two fingers, saying: "For me, he will always be the 'pejecito,' like this,
tiny." Those were terrible years. It was so sad to see how they boasted of an
electoral fraud with no apparent consequences for them.

But it is precisely that mistake, the gravest one of the opposition's cores in
Mexico, that sinks them. They belittle López Obrador by the book. They can
loathe him, abominate him, condemn him, curse him, despise him. To each their
own. But belittling him is underestimating him, and that has always had
devastating consequences for the right. It is there, in that mistake that is
an abyss, where the leader of the left grows stronger. It is there that the
arrogant elites lose, because they believe they can buy everything with money;
that they can fix everything with a check.

They belittle him because they are classists, and they indulge in being
classist with him because they think nothing happens; that they can fix
everything with their wallet and without consequences. It is clear that they
fix nothing.

López Obrador's recent appearance, this last one in particular, has that
connotation. He looks strong, physically and mentally. One never knows, but I
thought, as I watched him sitting in his rocking chair at La Chingada
announcing his new book, _Pueblo_ (Planeta 2026), that he is going to bury
many of his enemies. They belittle him and they summon him. They do not
understand that he prefers to write books, but if they provoke him, he will
return. And he will be implacable. And he can be implacable.

Those who speculate that there is a rupture with Claudia Sheinbaum are
mistaken, too; and so are those who bet that there is a subordination. I know
that at this point they do not care about making fools of themselves, and it
shows that they prefer hurling insults and lies to reflecting, but rest
assured that **every appearance of AMLO is agreed upon**. If they do not talk
it over, these are things that are understood. As Juan Gabriel would say: and
don't provoke him. Don't provoke him, because I see him returning to the
public plaza. If the President needed him, he would do it. And if Morena
needed him, he would do it. Don't provoke him, and much less belittle him,
because the old leader of the left is less old than Enrique Krauze, Carlos
Salinas, Felipe Calderón, Ricardo Salinas Pliego or Héctor Aguilar Camín
think.

However, they will not be able to restrain themselves. I know it. They will
provoke him and belittle him. There will be no shortage of another Claudio X.
senior who, looking at the camera, with his jaw trembling with hatred, calls
him "'pejecito,' like this, tiny." And that is where they lose, out of
arrogance. Because they believe they can buy everything; that they can fix
everything even if they are moved by classism. They believe nothing happens,
that they can fix everything with their wallet and without consequences. But
they fix nothing.

So get ready, then, because that old man they give up for dead will return to
the plazas if necessary. Get ready, because he has the strength to travel the
whole country once more, on foot if required. And get ready, because **if he
returns, he is going for all the marbles**. I guarantee it.

## 2\. The Defeat of the Stateless

María Lilly Téllez was among the first. In fact, the far-right Senator missed
seven ordinary sessions and one of the Permanent Commission to go to the
United States and take part in events of far-right groups, according to a
report by the **SinEmbargo** Data Unit with information as of last May 8
["Lilly Téllez's pro-Trump and far-right agenda intensifies during Senate
sessions," by Arturo Daen]. On each visit, I believe, _Fox News_ received her
so she could speak ill of Mexico. She kept doing it. Each time with less
impact in the Mexican media and even over there.

After her would come her employer, Ricardo Salinas Pliego. Then Alejandro
Moreno Cárdenas and others. The contacts of the three are very similar and
public. They make use of the Cuban diaspora –which serves Marco Rubio,
Secretary of State– although I don't know whether Lilly, Salinas Pliego and
"Alito" are useful to the Cubans, because their weight in Mexico shrinks year
after year.

Now the club of the stateless has problems, new problems: its great ally is
the US far right. It always has been, but now that it is in power it is not
only an ally: it is its support. Very recently this club, originally united by
its hatred of López Obrador, thought that Donald Trump's aggressive
interventionist agenda opened the opportunity of a lifetime for it. They
thought Mexico would surrender easily to MAGA. And the opposite happened.

Two facts. First: the Latinobarómetro confirmed last week what the Pew Center
had already warned, that **the rejection of Trump among Mexicans is the
highest in all of Latin America** ; their disapproval of Washington's foreign
policy is close to 79 percent, followed by Honduras, with 72; Guatemala, with
71; and Uruguay, with 70 percent. And second fact: it is highly likely that
MAGA and Trump will lose the Senate, which makes the removal of the US
president more real.

Both facts are terrible for the club of the stateless. They tied their own
political destiny to that of a sinking ship; they embraced Trump because they
wanted to take advantage of the far-right winds in their favor, without
knowing that Trump would head, through the thickest fog, toward an
archipelago. And I would say more: they have betrayed their country; they have
asked Washington to invade Mexican soil and they agreed to dance to the rhythm
it set for them.

They bet against Mexico, and they will be left with defeat and a tattoo on
their foreheads that says "TRAITORS."

## 3\. But What's the Need: Three Notes

One. How broad can Trump's defeat be in November? He has said the polls always
underestimate him, but even so, the US economy is so bad that in the coming
weeks it could sink further. New polls by _The New York Times_ and Siena
University one month before the elections say that voters' dissatisfaction
with the economy, concern about political extremism and frustration with Trump
have put the Democrats within reach of snatching four and even five
governorships that Republicans hold today. The Democrats have several paths to
regain the majority in the Senate, says _The New York Times_ , "despite a
complex electoral landscape that favored Republicans ahead of the midterm
elections." The Democrats need four seats from the Republicans and to hold
three in key states. Can it be done? A month ago, no. Today, yes, and the
outlook will most likely worsen for Trump in the coming weeks.

Two. Forgive me if I am so basic, but I can't stop thinking about that moment
in November when the United States wipes the smile off Ricardo Salinas Pliego,
Lilly Téllez, Alejandro Moreno Cárdenas and so many stateless people who would
like to see us subjugated to Washington, like Venezuela or like Iraq. I think
about that moment and I have to imagine it and I enjoy it. It lasted them so
little. It was a terrifying journey toward the far right that at some point
was going to stop and, it seems, it is now. They can still do Mexico a lot of
harm, of course. Nobody should celebrate victory yet. But November will be a
month to remember. They can still do Brazil harm, and I would tell it to
resist; that the Brazilian progressive forces do what they can democratically
do but stop any Trumpist attempt. That they resist a little longer. That they
not allow the mistake other peoples made. The far right is about to suffer a
hard blow to the back of the neck. A US majority is very close to putting a
dam on the outpouring of hatred. Resist. Resist. And I want to see the faces
of those others. I'll settle for imagining them.

Three. Many things stand out from AMLO's new book. One important one, which
all followers of his movement should learn, is the weight the direct
relationship with the people has for him; never detaching from the people. And
the other highlight is the messages he sends to Morena through _Pueblo_.
Popularity, López Obrador says, does not justify a candidacy. "If the
candidate with whom we can win is the husband or wife of the authority they
are going to replace, it is better to lose; if there is a very handsome or
witty, famous candidate with whom we can win, but there is evidence that he is
a crook, well, better not, what's the need," writes the former president. I
think it is a bit late for the 2027 election regarding candidates for
Governor, but not for the deputies. It seems to me that the governing party
has much to reflect on regarding its alliances; on the unprecedented power it
has given the Green Party even if it denies it, and on what those in the Labor
Party misunderstood, who now feel like birds shooting at the shotguns.
Morena's leadership needs to talk with itself and turn toward its membership.
It must learn to translate discontent into opportunity. If people say they are
not satisfied with the agreements with the Greens, it should revoke them.
That's what I think. But who am I: I just watch.
